title: Castor oil in the navel
summary: A few drops of quality castor oil in the belly button—traditional nabhi practice, ricinoleic acid context, safety, and how to log it.

sections.heading: What people do
sections.body: A few drops of high-quality, organic cold-pressed castor oil go into the belly button (navel), often before sleep. Some people cover the area with a soft cloth so oil does not stain sheets. In Ayurveda this appears among nabhi (navel) therapies; online it is sometimes called the pechoti or belly-button oil method. This article is external navel use only—not drinking castor oil, which is a much stronger laxative.

sections.heading: Why the navel, why castor
sections.body: The navel is the scar where the umbilical cord attached. It sits over dense abdominal networks of nerves and vessels. Traditional and lifestyle communities treat it as a convenient daily focal point—not because the navel “drinks” oil like a straw, but because the skin is thin, the spot is easy to repeat, and rituals stick. Castor oil is thick and rich in ricinoleic acid, a fatty acid with an extra hydroxyl group that makes it more polar than many plant oils. Advocates say that polarity interacts with skin and fascia water layers differently from generic massage oil. Castor is generally considered safer for routine topical use than DMSO, which can carry other substances through skin if misused.

sections.heading: Practical habit and safety
sections.body: Buy reputable cold-pressed castor oil (ricin is removed in commercial grades—never use raw beans). Patch-test on the inner arm. Use a clean dropper; 2–5 drops in a clean navel is typical. Stop for redness, itch, discharge, or pain. Skip if pregnant, if you have an umbilical hernia, or an open belly wound unless a clinician approves. Wash residue the next morning if needed.

sections.heading: What is solid vs framework
sections.body: Solid ground: castor oil is a traditional topical oil; ricinoleic acid chemistry is real; patch-testing and wound/pregnancy cautions are sensible. Framework / teaching layer: that navel castor oil meaningfully changes vagal tone, gut deuterium load, or lymphatic “drainage” in measurable ways. Dr. Jack Kruse–adjacent water and gut-support conversations sometimes place this habit in a low-cost stack while light, sleep, and food quality do the heavy lifting. Treat mechanism claims as teaching color, not proof.

sections.heading: How to use it here
sections.body: Log Vagus nerve stimulation → Castor oil navel when you complete your evening drop. Pair with Daylight-aligned hydration, deuterium-aware meals, and Earlier last meal if gut comfort is your goal—it does not replace morning light, grounding, or dark sleep. Educational only—not medical advice for bloating, IBD, or infection.
